The first thing the river returned was a shoe.

It appeared on the mudbank one April morning, upright and polished, though it had gone into the water thirteen years before. Mr. Vale recognized it by the crooked heel. His wife had lost it while crossing the bridge on their wedding day, and they had spent the rest of that day laughing about how she’d arrived at the reception with one bare foot.

By noon, everyone in town had come to see.

The river had always taken things. Umbrellas, fishing rods, a red bicycle, a whole section of fence during the flood of ’82. It had taken people, too, but nobody said that while they stood on the bank looking at the shoe.

The next April it returned a teaspoon. After that, a set of house keys, a child’s mitten, and a photograph so faded that no one could agree who was in it. One thing each year, on no particular day. The town learned to watch the mudbank when the water ran high.

My father kept a notebook of the returns. He measured the objects, made drawings, and wrote down every account of how they’d been lost. When I was small, I went with him to ask questions. He let me carry the notebook because he knew I liked being taken for his assistant.

“Why does it bring them back?” I asked once.

He was drawing the teaspoon. “I don’t know.”

“You know everything about the river.”

“I know where it’s shallow,” he said. “That’s different.”

He died in November, when I was thirty-six. That winter, I found the notebook among his things and brought it home. I meant to read it. Instead, I left it on the kitchen table under a stack of bills.

In April, the river returned a blue glass marble.

I found it before anyone else. Rain had made the bank slippery, and I had gone down there to clear my head after a difficult phone call. The marble was lying beside a clump of reeds, bright against the silt.

I knew it at once.

When I was nine, I had owned six marbles in a velvet pouch. Five were plain. This one had a twist of yellow through the middle. I carried it everywhere, until I dropped it from the bridge while trying to show my father how the yellow looked in sunlight. He had climbed down to search the shallows. I stood above him, angry that he couldn’t find it, and angrier still when he said it was time to go home.

I picked up the marble and wiped it on my coat. It was smooth and cold and no different from any marble you could buy for a few coins.

Mr. Vale saw me coming up the path. He was old by then and walked to the river most mornings.

“What’s it brought us?” he called.

I opened my hand. He leaned close, then gave a disappointed little smile.

“Do you know whose it is?”

“Mine.”

“Well,” he said. “That’s a bit of luck.”

News traveled anyway. By lunchtime three people had asked to see the marble, and the woman at the post office told me I must be glad to have something back from my father. I said yes because she meant well.

At home, I put the marble beside the notebook. For weeks I had been trying to remember the sound of my father’s laugh. I thought an object from our childhood might help, but all I could remember was him standing knee-deep in the river, looking down through the moving water. When I showed him the marble at nine, I had expected him to know exactly where it would land. I had expected him to bring it back.

That evening I opened his notebook. The first pages were careful: dates, dimensions, names. Over the years his handwriting loosened. He had begun adding details that had nothing to do with the returns. Beside the mitten, he had written that its owner was now grown and worked at the bakery. Beside the fence, he had noted that the flood had left three trout in the school playground.

On the last filled page was a drawing of the bridge. Under it he had written, *Went looking again. Too much water to see the bottom.*

There was no date. I read the line several times. Then I turned back through the notebook, looking for the marble, but found no mention of it.

The following morning, I went to the bridge. I had the marble in my pocket and the notebook under my arm. From the middle of the bridge, I could see Mr. Vale making his slow way along the bank. He raised a hand to me. I raised mine back.

I took out the marble. Its yellow twist caught the light, just as I remembered. For a moment I thought of dropping it in. My father had spent an afternoon searching for it and, perhaps, another morning many years later. I could leave it where he had wanted to find it.

Instead, I put it back in my pocket. I went down to the bank and walked with Mr. Vale until he needed to sit. He asked whether I’d found the marble a place to keep it.

“Not yet,” I said.

He pointed to the notebook. “Will you write it down?”

I opened to a clean page and wrote the date. Then I drew the marble, badly. Mr. Vale watched the river while I worked, and when I finished, he told me what he remembered about the shoe.
